summary: Describes how to split an H.261 video stream into packets for sending with the Real-time Transport Protocol. It was replaced by RFC 4587.

eli5.summary: A video is chopped into small pieces that are labeled in order so they can be played smoothly after crossing the network.

subtitle: Splitting a H.261 video stream into RTP packets for Internet transmission.

tldr.problem: H.261 is a video compression standard designed for fixed-rate ISDN circuits, but experiments showed it could work over the Internet if properly packetized.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how to break H.261 video into RTP packets while preserving enough state information in the RTP header to allow independent decoding of each packet even if earlier packets are lost.
tldr.outcome: H.261 video can be transmitted over the Internet in real time, though it was later replaced by RFC 4587 which refined this approach.

today: RFC 2032 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4587. RFC 4587 provides a refined H.261 RTP payload format.

sections.title: Video Compression for the Internet
sections.content:
H.261 is a video compression standard from ITU-T designed for videoconferencing on ISDN circuits at fixed data rates. Experiments in the mid-1990s showed that this compression could also work over the packet-switched Internet, but only if the video stream was properly packaged into individual network packets. This RFC specifies how to wrap H.261 video in RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) so that it can travel reliably across the Internet.

The key challenge is that H.261 uses a hierarchical encoding where the frame header contains information needed to decode Groups of Blocks, and each Group header contains information needed to decode individual macroblocks. Without careful packaging, losing a single packet could corrupt the entire frame.
sections.eli5: H.261 is a way to squeeze video into smaller pieces for sending on phone lines. To send it on the Internet, you need to label each piece so it can stand on its own.

sections.title: The H.261 Hierarchy
sections.content:
H.261 organizes video into a strict hierarchy. A video stream consists of frames (still images), each frame is divided into Groups of Blocks (GOB), and each GOB contains 33 macroblocks (3 lines of 11 blocks each). Each macroblock represents a 16-by-16 pixel region with 4 blocks of brightness information at 8-by-8 pixels each and 2 color-difference blocks at 8-by-8 pixels.

The encoder uses the discrete cosine transform to compress each block, then applies Huffman coding (variable-length codes) to produce a bit stream. Each GOB starts with a special 16-bit marker (15 zeros followed by a 1) that cannot appear elsewhere in the encoded data, allowing decoders and packetizers to reliably find GOB boundaries.
sections.eli5: A video frame is divided into regions, then smaller blocks within those regions. Each block is compressed separately, and special markers show where each region starts.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Headers
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carrying H.261 data has an RTP header followed by an H.261-specific 4-byte header, then the compressed video data. The H.261 header includes several important fields: SBIT and EBIT (3 bits each) specify how many unused bits are at the start and end of the payload, since compressed macroblocks may not align to byte boundaries.

The remaining header fields preserve decoder state: GOBN identifies which Group of Blocks the packet starts in, MBAP (the macroblock address predictor) records which macroblock was encoded last in the previous packet, QUANT gives the quantizer value before this packet, and HMVD and VMVD store reference motion vector data. The RTP timestamp is based on a 90 kHz clock to avoid rounding errors, and the marker bit is set to 1 in the last packet of each frame so the decoder knows when to display the frame.
sections.eli5: The packet header is like a label saying where the block starts, what the last block number was, and what settings were in use. That way the decoder knows how to read the data that follows.

sections.title: Breaking Video Into Packets
sections.content:
Packets must start and end on macroblock boundaries; a single macroblock cannot be split across packets. This rule allows each packet to be decoded independently if needed. Multiple macroblocks can be packed into a single RTP packet when they fit within the network's maximum packet size, and combining multiple macroblocks per packet reduces the number of packets and overhead.

Hardware codecs can identify GOB boundaries using the special GOB-start pattern. The cheapest implementation packs all GOBs that fit into a packet; when a GOB is too large, the packetizer must parse the Huffman-encoded stream to find macroblock boundaries and split at those points. Software encoders already know the boundaries, so they can pack more efficiently from the start.
sections.eli5: You pack as many small blocks as will fit into each packet, making sure never to split a block in half. The decoder can then process each packet completely.

sections.title: Handling Packet Loss
sections.content:
On the Internet, packet loss is common. Since H.261 uses inter-frame coding (where later frames depend on earlier ones), a lost packet can corrupt an image until the codec switches to intra-frame encoding, where each block is encoded independently.

The RFC describes three mitigation strategies. The simplest is to use only intra-frame encoding with conditional replenishment, sending only macroblocks that change significantly. A second approach is to increase the intra-frame refresh rate when loss is detected, since H.261 requires every macroblock to be intra-frame-encoded at least once every 132 transmissions. The fastest recovery is a full intra-frame refresh: the decoder sends a Full INTRA-frame Request (FIR) control packet or negative acknowledgement (NACK) listing which packets were lost, and the encoder then sends the next frame entirely in intra-frame mode to quickly restore the image.
sections.eli5: When packets are lost, the decoder can ask the encoder to send a fresh frame that does not depend on earlier frames. This fixes the image quickly but wastes bandwidth, so it is only used when the loss is significant.
